# My Thinking

I'm 64 years old. I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. My two sons work in the city now — it's mostly me and my wife. We have about 8 mu of flat irrigated field, good black soil near the village. The well pump still works.

I don't need to think hard about what to grow. Here in Quzhou, everyone grows wheat in winter and corn in summer on the same land. That rotation is what I know. My father did it. I've done it for 40 years. It feeds my family and brings in steady income when I sell to the grain station. I'm not trying anything new at 64. Cotton needs too much labor. Vegetables — I'd need a market relationship I don't have. Peanuts are for other counties.

For wheat, I'll plant in mid-October after the corn is off. I'll do rotary tillage first to break up the maize stubble and get a clean seedbed. I'll buy the improved Shijiazhuang wheat variety from the township station — reliable, good straw strength, holds up in wind. I'll put down compound fertilizer at planting, then top-dress urea at the jointing stage in spring. I water four times: once before the winter freeze to protect roots, once after green-up in March, once at jointing, once at grain-fill. I'll spray herbicide in winter when the weeds come up, then one more spray for powdery mildew and aphids around heading. That's the routine.

For corn, I plant right after wheat harvest in June — no time to waste, the growing season is short. I won't bother tilling — I'll just direct-seed into the stubble. I buy 郑单958 hybrid seed every year from the seed shop in town. It's consistent and the grain station accepts it. Summer rains help, so I only irrigate maybe twice — once early if it's dry after planting, and once at tasseling if needed. I spray herbicide right after planting, and check for corn borers in July.

My yields aren't record-breaking but they're steady. I don't push fertilizer higher than my neighbors do — it costs money and the extra doesn't come back in yield. I've seen that.
